title: I built a code-first C# game engine designed for coding agents
author: Arcodiant
selftext:
Hey folks!

I've just pre-released **Empyrean**, my C#/Vulkan game engine, on Nuget, and I'd love to get some feedback!

For the video, I asked Claude to build a game using Empyrean, with no prior knowledge of the engine beyond where to download it, and a prompt made from random words picked from WordNet.

You can see the result - a tower defense game about a diner using solar mirrors and a flash flood to defend itself against monster trucks. Claude was able to discover and use all the pieces it needed - lighting options, particle effects, ray-traced reflections, UI elements - without having to search the web for documentation or sample code.

The video shows the actual game running, along with prompts and responses from the agent session as Claude builds, tests and iterates on it. The footage is captured directly from the engine using the same tools Claude used to playtest. The clips at the end are from some of the other games I've been building as feature demos of the engine itself.

And that's one of the main goals of Empyrean: making the entire engine discoverable and usable through ordinary code and documentation, for both developers and coding agents.

So what's different?

1. Code-first

Many popular game engines revolve around a visual editor, with scripting as a separate part of the workflow. Empyrean is designed to work as a regular .NET project instead.

You can create an entire game from your IDE, using C# and human-readable content files, alongside your usual tools like Blender. I come from a software development background, so I wanted a game engine that felt familiar and used my existing dev process, with the same workflow, tools, version control and automation.

2. Designed for coding agents

The NuGet packages including documentation specifically designed for agents: API references, code samples, feature guides and detailed changelogs, all in markdown.

To get started, all you do is ask your agent to create a .NET 10 project, install Arcodiant.Empyrean, and read the bundled documentation.

There's no special MCP integration required; agents work with ordinary code and files, instead of trying to operate a graphical editor designed for humans.

The engine also provides tools for agents to run and playtest their games, capture and inspect rendered frames, and iterate on the results, along with built-in bug reporting and feature requests.

The idea is to make the whole dev process accessible to both humans and agents, without completely changing your way of working.

While Empyrean is designed with LLMs in mind, I want it to be a fully-capable, general-purpose game engine. Some highlights:

* Core: Scene-scoped ECS, game stages, asset loading and streaming, async jobs and tweening.
* Graphics: Vulkan renderer, glTF models, PBR materials, lighting and shadows, optional hardware ray tracing, HDR, post-processing, particles, and 2D sprites/tilemaps.
* Programmable rendering: Custom Slang/GLSL shaders, compute and render stages, custom pipelines and headless rendering.
* Gameplay: Skeletal animation, Jolt physics, navmesh navigation, audio mixing and 3D audio.
* UI and input: Retained and immediate-mode interfaces, keyboard/mouse/gamepad input, actions and gestures.
* VR/XR: OpenXR support, controller and hand tracking, and a synthetic runtime for testing without a headset.
* Diagnostics: Debug HUD, frame-time statistics, GPU/CPU metrics, frame capture and custom instrumentation.

If you want to try it out:

NuGet: [`Arcodiant.Empyrean`](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Arcodiant.Empyrean/)

Empyrean is currently distributed as NuGet packages under the MIT License, although the source repository isn't public at this stage. It currently supports Windows x64, with Linux support planned. As this is a pre-release, APIs are still subject to change before v1.0.

I'd love feedback from anyone who tries it with their own coding agent, or from C# developers interested in a code-first approach to game development.

If you run into problems or find something missing, let me know! (Or have Claude do it for you...)

comments.author: MrSuicideFish
comments.body: Probably not a great idea. You seem to be going backwards, most engines nowadays are visual because before (late 90s/ early 2000s) things were very code-centric. So developers created visual tools so designers could really capitalize  on their vision without needing Engineer support. We've seen engines introduce more and more visual tools not just for ease, but for designer control. Going back to the olden days of code-based editors probably wont get much traction in an age where designers are expecting maximum control.

replies.author: i_rate_slop
replies.body:
I disagree that they’re going backwards. We see more game engines introducing agent driven tooling and there’s engines like shallot designed entirely around agents driving without a visual editor at all.

We’re entering an era of natural language driven iteration. If you need a way to visualize something, just ask for a tool to visualize it and wait an hour.

I don’t look at Unity or UE anymore. I look at the actual built game.

replies.author: MrSuicideFish
replies.body: Agent driven tooling is fine and has already been the case for engines with a pre-existing editor API. But PURE agent-driven tooling is already out-of-date. We did an experiment last year for MCP based tool-architecture and it turns out that some devs don't know what they don't know. Devs would frequently reinvent the wheel with less features. Features that only came about due to rigorous community feedback and testing. The answer moving forward seems to be some mix of pre-existing editor tools and API with a robust MCP layer. Especially for beginners.

comments.author: Brave-History-6502
comments.body:
Interesting idea-- I was playing around with a more agent designed engine as a part of a cloud game dev proejct I'm working on but it was such a black hole -- there are just so many edge cases with engines.

This looks cool though.. How long have you been working on it?

replies.author: Arcodiant
replies.body:
I've been working on lots of different engines over the years 😄 but this iteration started about 8 months ago.

I get what you mean about the edge cases; what I've ended up doing is building a plan & implement plugin that lets me spin up the core vertical of a game remake (like Minecraft, or Balatro, or X-COM) and where they find bugs or missing features, I have the automated request process to submit from the game dev agents, and add to the backlog for the engine dev agents.

replies.author: Brave-History-6502
replies.body:
I was working on a purely vibe coded engine intended to have interfaces designed for agents with rust. But it was too much a time suck (and huge pit for tokens) and not my main focus. 

Kind of works but in benchmarks I couldnt get the agent even close to llm performance in game creation. Some aspects were much faster but overall the output was mediocre at best.

Trying to find a better option than godot, unity, three js for my tool: gamecrew.ai

Would love to try out yours once you feel like it’s really ready/closer to v1 since I think there is ton of advantage to an engine built from the ground up for agentic use.
